meta.about: Knowledge base for ShredLog: budget protein tips, micronutrient gaps, food-to-symptom hints, quick Indian meals.

priceBasisLegend.listing: priced from a retail/wholesale listing or official price series seen during research (see src, priceNote)
priceBasisLegend.range-midpoint: midpoint of several retail quotes / the brief range
priceBasisLegend.estimate: no direct listing retrievable; typical Indian retail estimate, verify before relying on it

meta.inrPer10gProteinFormula: priceInr / gramsPerUnit * 1000 / (proteinPer100g * ediblePct/100); i.e. rupees to buy 10 g of protein as purchased (dry weight for dals, raw weight for meat). Sorted ascending.
caveats: Prices are indicative metro retail and move weekly; whey prices rose sharply in 2026 on an imported-whey shortage.
Many price pages are undated aggregator listings (BigBasket, IndiaMART, rate sites). Government dal series (PIB / Dept of Consumer Affairs) are dated 2024-25.
Nutrient values are rounded IFCT 2017 / NIN Nutritive Value of Indian Foods figures with USDA FDC as fallback; real foods vary by variety, cooking and fortification.
RDA values come from secondary summaries of ICMR-NIN 2020 (FSSAI RDA 2021 and the Aug 2021 amendment); the primary NIN table could not be fetched. Folate values in particular should be confirmed.
Symptom hints are general tips, not medical advice. See a doctor for persistent symptoms, blood in stool, unexplained weight loss or severe pain.

derived at runtime by js/insights.js.large_meal: meal kcal well above your median

behaviour tags the app must derive or lo.low_water_high_protein: high-protein day with low water intake
behaviour tags the app must derive or lo.fiber_jump: fibre up by more than about 10 g/day versus the previous week

meta.symptomIdNote: symptom uses the brief vocabulary; appSymptom is the matching id in js/insights.js SYMPTOMS (constipation -> hard_stool).
meta.mealFixesNote: fixes follow the brief ('b12'); B12 meals also carry 'vitamin_b12' because js/insights.js builds gap ids from micro ids.
meta.measuresNote: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines 2024 standard measuring set: katori 115/155/200/360 ml (155 ml ~ 150 ml katori used here); 5 g per teaspoon of oil (4.5 g used here for level tsp of liquid oil); roti 40 g cooked medium (about 30 g flour) is a common-practice value; official annexure values were not re-verified.

proteinSources.name: Soya chunks (Nutrela)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Soaked/boiled weight is about 2.5x, so roughly 20 g protein per 100 g soaked.
proteinSources.notes: Soak in hot water 15 min and squeeze out the water; discarding it cuts the beany taste and bloating. Pair with roti or rice.
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket Rs 123/kg, Zepto Rs 139/kg, MRP Rs 150-190; bulk 25 kg bags Rs 75-100/kg ex-tax. Rs 130 = mid retail.

proteinSources.name: Masoor dal (red lentil, split)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked dal is mostly water: about 7-9 g protein per 100 g thick dal, 4-5 g per watery katori.
proteinSources.notes: Cooks in 15 min with no soaking and is easy on the stomach. Pair with rice or roti to complete the amino acids.
proteinSources.priceNote: Bharat masoor dal Rs 89/kg (govt, PIB Mar 2025); 2024 all-India modal retail Rs 90/kg. Rs 95 allows a small retail premium.

proteinSources.name: Besan (chana flour)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry flour. 2 besan chillas use about 60 g flour (about 13 g protein).
proteinSources.notes: Make chilla or pudla with veg and little oil. Cook through; half-cooked besan causes gas.
proteinSources.priceNote: No clean per-kg retail listing found (pack prices Rs 68-76 for mixed sizes); estimate from chana dal retail (Rs 85-100/kg) plus milling.

proteinSources.name: Kala chana (black chickpea)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Boiled kala chana is about 9 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Soak 8-12 h, discard the water and pressure cook. High fibre keeps you full; start with half a katori to avoid gas.
proteinSources.priceNote: Bharat chana whole Rs 58/kg (Oct 2024 govt); all-India modal chana Rs 85/kg (May 2024). Rs 90 = current retail estimate.

proteinSources.name: Chana dal (split Bengal gram)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked dal is roughly 8 g protein per 100 g thick, 4-5 g per watery katori.
proteinSources.notes: Low glycaemic index. Soak 2-3 h and cook with hing and jeera; swap to moong if it makes you gassy.
proteinSources.priceNote: Govt retail average about Rs 88.7/kg (Sep, DoCA snapshot); Bharat chana dal Rs 70/kg (Oct 2024). Rs 100 per your range.

proteinSources.name: Moong dal (split yellow)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked moong dal is about 7 g protein per 100 g thick dal.
proteinSources.notes: The easiest dal to digest and good for a light dinner. Whole green moong (sabut) is cheaper and higher in fibre.
proteinSources.priceNote: Govt retail average about Rs 112/kg (DoCA snapshot); Bharat moong dal Rs 107/kg. Market packs Rs 120-150.

proteinSources.name: Urad dal (split black gram)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked urad dal is about 8 g protein per 100 g thick dal.
proteinSources.notes: Heavier on the stomach: cook with ginger and hing. Fermented in idli/dosa batter it causes less gas.
proteinSources.priceNote: All-India modal retail urad Rs 120/kg (May 2024); no 2025-26 national snapshot found. Rs 125 estimate.

proteinSources.name: Toor / arhar dal
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked toor dal is about 7 g protein per 100 g thick dal.
proteinSources.notes: Everyday sambar/dal. A bit gassier than moong or masoor; pressure cook well and add hing.
proteinSources.priceNote: Govt retail average about Rs 125.7/kg (DoCA snapshot); market packs Rs 130-160.

proteinSources.name: Peanuts (raw, shelled)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Roasted/boiled differs slightly. 30 g handful = 170 kcal and 7.6 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: Calorie-dense: great for bulking, easy to overeat on a cut. Peanut-jaggery chikki is a cheap snack.
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket packaged raw peanuts Rs 190-206/kg; Hyperpure Rs 160/kg; loose kirana typically Rs 130-160/kg. Rs 160 = lower retail band.

proteinSources.name: Sattu (roasted chana flour)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry powder. 2 tbsp (30 g) in water gives about 6 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: No-cook drink: mix with water, lemon, jeera and salt. Big servings can cause gas or acidity; start small.
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket BB Royal sattu Rs 128/kg; Patna retail Rs 140/kg; sweetened ready mixes cost far more and are not counted.

proteinSources.name: Rajma (kidney beans)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Boiled rajma is about 8.7 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: High-FODMAP: soak 8-12 h, discard the water, pressure cook until very soft. Keep to 1/2-1 katori at first.
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket Rajdhani Srinagar rajma Rs 153/kg (Rs 96 per 500 g).

proteinSources.name: Kabuli chana (chole)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Boiled chole is about 8.9 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Soak 8-12 h, discard water. Canned, drained and rinsed chickpeas are the lowest-FODMAP form.
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket: bb Royal Rs 141/kg, Tata Sampann Rs 180/kg, Royals Kitchen Rs 239/kg; 500 g budget packs about Rs 140-156/kg. Rs 140 = value brand.

proteinSources.name: Whole eggs (farm)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: About 50 g edible per egg = 6.5 g protein. Hard-boiled egg is similar per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Best all-round budget complete protein: about 6.5 g per Rs 7. Keep the yolk for B12, vitamin D and choline.
proteinSources.priceNote: NECC wholesale about Rs 5.8-6.6/egg (mKisan, KisanDeals; Delhi Rs 6.3 on 23 Oct 2026). Retail runs 10-25% above NECC, so Rs 7/egg x 30 = Rs 210.

proteinSources.name: Skimmed milk powder
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 30 g powder in 250 ml water gives about 10 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: A cheap protein booster for oats, lassi or shakes. Contains lactose (about 50% by weight).
proteinSources.priceNote: No listing retrieved (src null); about Rs 400-500/kg is the typical retail range.

proteinSources.name: Chicken breast (boneless)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Raw weight. Cooked breast is about 31 g protein and 165 kcal per 100 g (about 30% water loss).
proteinSources.notes: Very lean; do not overcook. Bone-in chicken costs less per kg but you pay for the bone.
proteinSources.priceNote: Bengaluru price guide Rs 360-450/kg; Hyperpure boneless breast 2 kg Rs 575 (about Rs 288/kg wholesale). Rs 340 = mid of your Rs 300-380 band.

proteinSources.name: Rolled oats
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked in water (1:2) is about 4 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Good fibre (beta-glucan) but low protein density; cook in milk or add whey/curd to make it a protein meal.
proteinSources.priceNote: IndiaMART rolled oats Rs 220/kg; branded retail typically Rs 180-230/kg.

proteinSources.name: Tofu (firm)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Firm pressed tofu 14-18 g protein per 100 g; silken tofu is only 5-8 g.
proteinSources.notes: Low-lactose, soy-based; scramble as bhurji or grill. Keeps 3-4 days refrigerated.
proteinSources.priceNote: Pro Plant tofu 200 g at Rs 53 (about Rs 265/kg, 18 g protein claim) seen in a retail comparison table; no stable product URL, so src is null.

proteinSources.name: Peanut butter (unsweetened)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 tbsp (15 g) = about 3.8 g protein and 90 kcal.
proteinSources.notes: Choose 90%+ peanuts with no added sugar or palm oil. Very calorie-dense: measure the spoon.
proteinSources.priceNote: Branded unsweetened peanut butter typically Rs 350-550/kg; no listing retrieved (src null).

proteinSources.name: Chicken, whole (with skin and bone)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Per 100 g EDIBLE meat+skin. About 65% of the purchased weight is edible, so 100 g purchased gives about 12.7 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: Cheaper per kg, but about a third is bone. Skin adds fat: remove it for a cut.
proteinSources.priceNote: Dressed-chicken retail about Rs 200-260/kg in metros (rate sites); no single retrievable listing, so Rs 230 is an estimate.

proteinSources.name: Toned milk
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 litre weighs about 1,030 g. 1 glass (250 ml) = 8 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: Lactose: choose curd or paneer over milk if you bloat. 2 glasses (500 ml) give about 16 g protein.
proteinSources.priceNote: Mother Dairy pouched toned Rs 57 (Apr-May 2025) rising to about Rs 60 after the May 2026 hike; Amul bulk toned Rs 55. Rs 58 = mid.

proteinSources.name: Desi (country) eggs
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: About 40 g edible per desi egg = 5.2 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: Smaller and pricier (about Rs 9-12 each); nutritionally close to farm eggs, so it is mostly a taste premium.
proteinSources.priceNote: Retail premium of about Rs 3-5 per egg over farm eggs; no systematic listing found.

proteinSources.name: Egg whites
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: About 33 g white per egg = 3.6 g protein. Cooked whites are similar per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Cost assumes you bought whole eggs; if you also eat the yolks (bhurji) the effective cost halves. Cook whites; raw whites block biotin.
proteinSources.priceNote: Derived from whole-egg price (Rs 7/egg) with yolks counted as waste; there is no standard Indian retail price for whites.

proteinSources.name: Paneer, low-fat
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 100 g = about 19 g protein and 190 kcal, versus about 290 kcal for full-fat.
proteinSources.notes: Good cut-phase swap: similar protein, 35% fewer calories. Fresh paneer has little lactose.
proteinSources.priceNote: Hyperpure wholesale Amul Lite paneer 500 g Rs 168 (about Rs 336/kg); retail markup brings it to about Rs 380/kg.

proteinSources.name: Full-cream milk
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 glass (250 ml) = about 8 g protein and 230 kcal.
proteinSources.notes: Lactose applies, same as toned milk. Higher calories help bulking; toned is better on a cut.
proteinSources.priceNote: Amul Gold Rs 67 (May 2025), Mother Dairy full cream Rs 69 (2025) rising to about Rs 72 (May 2026). Rs 70 = mid.

proteinSources.name: Fish (rohu)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Per 100 g EDIBLE flesh. About 55% of a whole rohu is edible after scaling, gutting and bones.
proteinSources.notes: Cheap freshwater fish; good B12. Fatty marine fish (bangda, sardine) give more omega-3 and vitamin D.
proteinSources.priceNote: Retail Delhi Rs 175/kg, Chennai Rs 205/kg, Raipur online Rs 210/kg; wholesale Rs 145-186/kg (Apr 2025).

proteinSources.name: Curd / dahi (toned, packaged)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Hung curd (strained overnight) is about 6-8 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Lactose is partly fermented, so curd is usually tolerated better than milk. Hang it for thick, higher-protein dahi.
proteinSources.priceNote: Pack prices for toned dahi (400 g pouches about Rs 30-35) imply about Rs 75-85/kg; no single listing fetched. Same dairy price class as Amul/Mother Dairy milk (source).

proteinSources.name: Paneer (full-fat)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Pack labels vary from 14 to 20 g protein per 100 g depending on moisture and brand.
proteinSources.notes: Whey is drained off, so lactose is low: usually fine when milk bloats you. Calorie-dense (100 g about 290 kcal).
proteinSources.priceNote: BigBasket Amul fresh paneer 1 kg Rs 435, Amul Malai block Rs 455; Mother Dairy Calcutta list Rs 300 (stale). GST on paneer cut to 0% from 22 Sep 2025.

proteinSources.name: Sprouts (moong / mixed)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Home 1-day sprouts are 8-11 g protein per 100 g; long-tailed market sprouts are only about 3-5 g (mostly water).
proteinSources.notes: Raw sprouts cause gas and carry bacteria risk: steam or saute for 5 minutes with lemon and jeera.
proteinSources.priceNote: Ready packs about Rs 35-45 per 250 g (Rs 140-180/kg); home sprouting costs about Rs 15-20/kg of moong equivalent.

proteinSources.name: Quinoa
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Dry weight. Cooked quinoa is about 4.4 g protein per 100 g.
proteinSources.notes: Complete protein but expensive for what it gives; jowar, bajra and ragi are far cheaper fibre sources.
proteinSources.priceNote: Online retail Rs 350/kg (Oct 2026 list); Selina Wamucii metros Rs 680-900/kg; bulk wholesale Rs 90/kg.

proteinSources.name: Cheese (processed block / slices)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 slice (20 g) = about 4 g protein and 60 kcal.
proteinSources.notes: Very little lactose but high in sodium and fat; fine as a topping, a poor main protein source.
proteinSources.priceNote: Amul processed cheese blocks retail about Rs 550-650/kg (estimate); src is the paneer listing as a dairy-retail reference.

proteinSources.name: Whey blend (budget, about 55% protein)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: A 45 g scoop gives about 24 g protein, with extra carbs, flavour and often sweeteners.
proteinSources.notes: Cheapest whey per kg but only 53-60% protein and often sweetened; compare cost per gram of protein, not per kg.
proteinSources.priceNote: Nakpro Impact Rs 1,599/kg (53% protein), AS-IT-IS ATOM Rs 1,792/kg (60%), Oct 2026.

proteinSources.name: Prawns (jhinga)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Per 100 g EDIBLE meat. About 65% of shell-on weight is edible.
proteinSources.notes: Low calorie and high protein but cholesterol-rich; shellfish allergy is common.
proteinSources.priceNote: Retail jhinga Delhi Rs 355/kg, New Delhi Rs 390, Chennai Rs 400 (Oct 2026 aggregator); peeled/jumbo costs far more.

proteinSources.name: Whey protein concentrate (plain)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 scoop (30-35 g) gives 24-28 g protein; protein by weight 73-80%.
proteinSources.notes: Lactose is present (about 3-4 g per scoop): if it bloats you, try isolate. Check for lab-tested labels.
proteinSources.priceNote: Oct 2026: Nakpro Whey Gold Rs 2,999/kg, AS-IT-IS ONE Rs 3,299, MuscleBlaze Raw Rs 3,499. Prices rose sharply in 2026 on imported-whey shortage (Business Standard).

proteinSources.name: Soy milk (unsweetened, fortified)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 glass (250 ml) = about 8 g protein.
proteinSources.notes: Pick unsweetened, calcium and B12 fortified. Mild bloating in some people.
proteinSources.priceNote: No retrievable listing; typical Indian soy-milk cartons Rs 120-160 per litre (estimate).

proteinSources.name: Whey protein isolate
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: 1 scoop (30 g) gives about 25-27 g protein; protein by weight 85-90%.
proteinSources.notes: Lowest lactose of the whey family, the best pick for milk-related bloating. Premium price.
proteinSources.priceNote: No pure isolate listing found in the Oct 2026 table (only blends); Business Standard cites whey up to Rs 4,500+/kg and isolate up about 5x since 2023. Rs 4,800 is an estimate.

proteinSources.name: Mutton (goat, bone-in)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Per 100 g EDIBLE meat. About 80% of bone-in weight is edible meat and fat.
proteinSources.notes: Rich in iron, zinc and B12 but costly per gram of protein and high in saturated fat. Use as a 1-2x/week iron booster.
proteinSources.priceNote: Retail Delhi Rs 815/kg, Chennai Rs 855, New Delhi Rs 875, UP Rs 785 (Oct 2026); supermarkets and apps Rs 980-1,180.

proteinSources.name: Greek yogurt (Epigamia, plain)
proteinSources.gramsPer100g_cooked_note: Epigamia plain is about 7 g protein per 100 g; Turbo high-protein line is about 12 g per 100 g (Rs 325 for 430 g).
proteinSources.notes: Convenient and low-lactose (strained) but about 9x the cost per gram of protein of eggs. Hang regular curd for a cheap version.
proteinSources.priceNote: Blinkit: 400 g Rs 250 (about Rs 625/kg); 85 g Rs 60.

micros.name: Iron
micros.ulNote: Tolerable upper limit about 45 mg/day (IOM/NIN). Do not supplement without a blood test (Hb, ferritin): excess causes GI upset and is risky in haemochromatosis.
micros.whyItMatters: Carries oxygen to working muscle; low iron means early fatigue, breathlessness on sets and slow recovery.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: NFHS-5 (2019-21): 57% of women and 25% of men aged 15-49 are anaemic.
micros.vegNote: Plant (non-haem) iron absorbs only about 2-10%. Squeeze lemon or amla on dal, chole and palak, keep chai/coffee 1 hour away from meals, and cook in an iron kadhai.
micros.rdaNote: ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020 (RDA, adult 18-50 y), as adopted by FSSAI RDA 2021 / Aug 2021 amendment.

micros.name: Calcium
micros.ulNote: Upper limit about 2,500 mg/day from food + supplements (NIN/IOM). Supplements above about 500 mg per dose absorb poorly: split doses and take with food.
micros.whyItMatters: Bone density and muscle contraction; heavy lifters and people who sweat a lot lose more calcium.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: No recent national adult survey found; older NNMB state surveys showed mean intakes of only about 280-400 mg/day (1970s data, dated) against the 1,000 mg RDA.
micros.vegNote: Vegans: ragi, til, methi/moringa leaves and calcium-set tofu or fortified soy milk. Spinach calcium is mostly oxalate-bound, so do not count on palak. Vitamin D improves absorption.
micros.rdaNote: ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020 (RDA, adult 18-50 y), as adopted by FSSAI RDA 2021 / Aug 2021 amendment.

topFoods.name: Sardine fish eaten with bones (tarli / canned)

micros.name: Vitamin D
micros.ulNote: Upper limit 100 mcg (4,000 IU)/day (IOM/NIN). Test 25(OH)D before high-dose supplements; weekly 60,000 IU sachets only under medical advice.
micros.whyItMatters: Supports calcium absorption, bone strength, muscle function and immunity; low levels link to aches and slower recovery.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: Pune corporate-employee study (vegetarians, n=100): 82% were vitamin D deficient; a larger pan-India diagnostic-lab dataset reports about 81% (self-selected samples).
micros.vegNote: Almost no veg food has vitamin D: rely on 15-30 min of midday sun on arms/legs 3-4x a week (darker skin needs longer), fortified milk/oil, and a supplement if tests are low. Vegans: choose D3 from lichen or D2.
micros.rdaNote: Vitamin D RDA 600 IU = 15 mcg/day (ICMR-NIN 2020). Food values vary widely by species, season and fortification.

micros.name: Vitamin B12
micros.ulNote: No upper limit set (excess is excreted). High-dose tablets or injections are for diagnosed deficiency under a doctor.
micros.whyItMatters: Needed for red blood cells and nerves; low B12 causes tiredness, tingling and poor workout recovery.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: In Pune men, vegetarians had 4.4x the risk of low B12 vs frequent non-veg eaters; a Pune vegetarian corporate sample found 14% B12-deficient.
micros.vegNote: B12 is almost absent in plant foods. Dairy and eggs help but often fall short, so vegetarians should get B12 tested; vegans must take a supplement or fortified foods (typical maintenance about 250 mcg/day, per doctor advice).
micros.rdaNote: ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020 (RDA, adult 18-50 y), as adopted by FSSAI RDA 2021 / Aug 2021 amendment.

micros.name: Vitamin C
micros.ulNote: Upper limit 2,000 mg/day (IOM). Over 1 g/day in supplements can cause loose stools and raises kidney-stone risk in prone people.
micros.whyItMatters: Collagen and tendon repair, immunity, and it multiplies absorption of plant iron.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: Household surveys show fruit+veg intake of only about 160-184 g/person/day (NSS 2011-12) vs the WHO 400 g; one survey found 98% of adults eat under 400 g. No national vitamin C deficiency survey.
micros.vegNote: Heat destroys vitamin C, so eat fruit and salads raw or lightly cooked. Lemon on dal/chole/palak can boost plant-iron absorption 2-3x.
micros.rdaNote: Vitamin C RDA 80 mg men / 65 mg women (ICMR-NIN 2020). Food values depend on variety and ripeness.

micros.name: Zinc
micros.ulNote: Upper limit 40 mg/day (IOM). Long-term high-dose supplements can cause copper deficiency and nausea.
micros.whyItMatters: Testosterone, protein synthesis and immunity; sweat losses are high in gym-goers.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: Share of Indians with inadequate absorbable zinc intake rose from 17.1% (1983) to 24.6% (2011-12), per Smith et al; CNNS 2016-18 found 32% of adolescents zinc-deficient.
micros.vegNote: Phytates in grains and legumes block zinc: soak, sprout or ferment (idli, dosa, sprouted moong). Vegetarians may need up to 50% more. Seeds, cashew and soya are the best plant sources.
micros.rdaNote: ICMR-NIN Nutrient Requirements for Indians 2020 (RDA, adult 18-50 y), as adopted by FSSAI RDA 2021 / Aug 2021 amendment.

micros.name: Magnesium
micros.ulNote: The 350 mg/day upper limit applies to supplements only (IOM); food magnesium has no limit. Excess supplement causes loose stools.
micros.whyItMatters: Muscle relaxation, cramps, sleep quality and energy metabolism.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: No national magnesium survey. A 2024 Lancet Global Health 185-country model flagged Indian men as more likely than women to have inadequate magnesium intake (no India-wide percentage published in coverage).
micros.vegNote: Plant foods are the main source, so vegetarians do well if they eat seeds, millets, greens and legumes. Sweating, alcohol and heavy chai can lower stores.
micros.rdaNote: Magnesium RDA 440/370 mg per the Aug 2021 FSSAI amendment of ICMR-NIN 2020 values (original July 2021 draft had 385/325).

micros.name: Potassium
micros.ulNote: No upper limit for food. If you have kidney disease or take ACE inhibitors/potassium-sparing drugs, check with a doctor before supplements or KCl salt substitutes.
micros.whyItMatters: Offsets sodium, reduces cramps and water retention, and supports muscle contraction.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: PGIMER/George Institute study (Frontiers in Nutrition 2024) of 404 north-Indian adults (182 healthy, 222 with CKD; no group difference): mean potassium intake only 1.43 g/day by 24-h urine vs the 3.5 g target.
micros.vegNote: Plant diets are naturally high in potassium; dal, rajma, banana, coconut water and sabzi do the job. Boiling in water leaches it, so use the cooking water.
micros.rdaNote: Potassium 3,510 mg/day adequate intake (ICMR-NIN 2020). Mean intake is typically far lower.

micros.name: Folate (vitamin B9)
micros.ulNote: Upper limit 1,000 mcg/day of synthetic folic acid (IOM). High folic acid can mask B12 deficiency, so test B12 too.
micros.whyItMatters: Red-cell and DNA synthesis; supports recovery and energy. Important before and during pregnancy.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: CNNS 2016-18: folate deficiency in 37% of Indian adolescents (government report) or 35.6% in a peer-reviewed analysis; 23% of pre-schoolers.
micros.vegNote: Dals, chana, rajma and green leafy vegetables are rich in folate, so most vegetarians do well. Overcooking and discarding cooking water destroys it: pressure cook pulses, lightly cook greens.
micros.rdaNote: Folate RDA 300 mcg DFE men / 220 mcg women as given in secondary summaries of ICMR-NIN 2020; one source lists 220 for both. Verify against the NIN table before clinical use.

micros.name: Dietary fibre
micros.ulNote: No upper limit, but raising fibre faster than about 5 g/week without enough water causes gas, bloating and constipation.
micros.whyItMatters: Keeps you full on a cut, supports gut regularity and steadier blood sugar.
micros.indiaPrevalenceNote: An industry survey (Aashirvaad, 2026; brand-sponsored) found nearly 7 in 10 Indians fall short of recommended fibre.
micros.vegNote: Most vegetarian staples (dal, sabzi, whole-grain roti, millets) already supply fibre. Maida, white rice and packaged snacks do not. Raise slowly and drink more water.
micros.rdaNote: Fibre RDA 30 g men / 25 g women for sedentary work; 40 g / 30 g for moderate work (ICMR-NIN 2020 via FSSAI). Active gym-goers should aim for the higher figure.

symptomHints.hint: Beans and chana ferment in the gut and cause gas. Soak 8-12 h, discard the water, pressure-cook until soft, add hing + jeera. Build portions up slowly.
Rajma and chole are high-FODMAP. Soak 8-12 h, discard water, pressure cook, add hing + jeera.
Urad, chana and toor dal ferment more than moong or masoor. Pressure-cook with hing, ginger and jeera, or switch to moong or masoor if gassy.
High-FODMAP foods (rajma, chole, cauliflower, onion-heavy gravies) bloat sensitive guts. Cut portions in half for 2 weeks and see if it settles.
Milk, milk powder and whey concentrate carry lactose. If you bloat within hours, try curd, paneer or whey isolate, or take milk in smaller glasses.
symptomHints.context: Lactose malabsorption is common in India (about 27% in a New Delhi cohort vs 67% in South Indian centres, 1981 study).

symptomHints.hint: Loose stools after milk or a whey-concentrate shake often point to lactose. Swap to isolate or lactose-free milk for a week and see if it clears.
Cheap whey blends often carry sweeteners and fillers that cause gas. If a shake bothers you, test plain concentrate or isolate for two weeks.
Paneer, curd and cheese have far less lactose than milk, so most people who bloat on milk tolerate them. If you still bloat, look at the onion-garlic gravy.
Whey and milk can worsen acne in some people. If breakouts follow, try 2-4 weeks off whey, or use isolate, plant protein, eggs and dal.
Some people bloat from wheat (fructans). If roti triggers you, try ragi, bajra or jowar roti for a week and compare.
Fried and oily food slows stomach emptying and can trigger heartburn. Air-fry or shallow-fry, keep portions small, stay upright 2-3 h after eating.
Heavy fried meals leave you sluggish for hours. Keep them away from pre-workout meals; pair with salad and a short walk afterwards.
Very spicy food and raw chilli can trigger heartburn. Cut chilli, add curd or raita, and avoid it close to bedtime.
A big plate of white rice spikes then drops blood sugar, causing a 2-3 pm slump. Halve the rice, start with dal or salad, add protein.
symptomHints.context: Large rice portion (about 250 g cooked or more) at lunch.

symptomHints.hint: One very large meal makes you drowsy. Split the same food into two sittings and add a 10-minute walk.
Eating within 2-3 hours of bed can keep you restless. Move dinner earlier, or make it light: dal, khichdi, egg whites or curd.
symptomHints.context: Meal within about 3 h of bedtime (app tag late_night = after 10 pm).

symptomHints.hint: Lying down soon after a heavy dinner pushes acid up. Leave 3 hours before bed; a short walk after eating helps.
Caffeine lingers 5-6 hours. Chai or coffee after 4 pm can cut sleep even if you drop off easily. Switch to haldi milk or herbal tea.
Tea or coffee with meals blocks iron absorption, a big deal for vegetarians. Keep chai 1 hour away from meals, or add lemon or amla to the meal.
symptomHints.context: Chai/coffee within about 1 hour of a meal, repeated for weeks.

symptomHints.hint: Sweets and sugary drinks spike then crash blood sugar, leaving you tired. Have them after a protein-rich meal, not on an empty stomach.
Sugary snacks often trigger more cravings an hour or two later. Pair sweets with protein, like nuts, curd or paneer, to blunt the swing.
Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night and cuts REM. Stop drinking at least 3 hours before bed.
Alcohol dehydrates you and often brings a next-morning headache. Alternate each drink with water and have nimbu pani or ORS before sleep.
High protein with little water and fibre slows the gut. Drink 2.5-3 L water, add isabgol, veggies and fruit; do not live on paneer and eggs alone.
symptomHints.context: High-protein day (about 1.6 g/kg or more) with low water and fibre.

symptomHints.hint: Low-fibre days (maida, white rice, no veg or dal) slow digestion. Aim for 25-30 g fibre: salad, fruit, dal and whole-grain roti.
Jumping fibre overnight (big salads, sattu, oats, bran) causes gas and bloating. Add about 5 g a week and drink more water.
symptomHints.context: Fibre intake rises by more than about 10 g/day in a week.

symptomHints.hint: Soya chunks and soy milk bloat some people. Squeeze out the soaking water, start with 25 g dry, and cook with ajwain or jeera.
Raw sprouts are hard to digest and can carry bacteria. Steam or saute 5 minutes, add lemon and jeera, and start with half a katori.
Onion and garlic are high-FODMAP and bloat some people. Try hing in the tadka, the green tops of spring onion, or garlic-infused oil.
Sorbitol, xylitol and other sugar alcohols in protein bars and sugar-free drinks ferment in the gut. Check labels; stevia and erythritol are usually gentler.
Salty namkeen, chips and papad hold water, so you feel puffy and the scale jumps. Balance with extra water and potassium: banana, coconut water.
Cutting carbs hard can cause headache in the first 1-2 weeks. Drink water, add salt and potassium (coconut water), and taper carbs gradually.
symptomHints.context: Under about 50 g carbs/day, first 1-2 weeks.

symptomHints.hint: Expect low energy and weaker workouts for 1-2 weeks on very low carb. Keep some carbs around the workout, or taper down instead of cutting at once.
Creatine pulls water into muscle: 0.5-1.5 kg on the scale in week 1 is normal. Take 3-5 g daily and drink water; it is not fat.
Nicotine suppresses appetite, so you may under-eat protein, then overeat later. Set meal times and a protein target instead of waiting for hunger.
Smoking, especially close to bedtime, is linked with lighter, poorer sleep. Avoid cigarettes for 2 hours before bed.
Smoking is linked with lower endurance and poorer sleep, so you may tire faster and recover slower. Many people notice better gym stamina within weeks of cutting down.
symptomHints.context: Evidence on recovery specifically is limited; treat as a likely, not proven, effect.
